title: Conservatives stunned by 'catastrophic' midterm blue tsunami, blame Trump's Iran war, high gas prices
text:
The 'Ruthless Podcast' co-hosts analyze Democrats' reported sweep in the 2026 midterm elections, including control of the House and Senate, on 'FOX News Democracy 26.'

Conservatives were left stunned by the results of the 2026 midterm elections Tuesday and are attempting to grapple with the new political landscape.

Democrats dominated in red and blue states alike, easily retaking both the House and Senate, as well as flipping several governorships. Democrats picked up victories in numerous states won by President Donald Trump in 2024, including seemingly deep-red spots like Texas, South Carolina and Kansas.

Members of conservative media were gobsmacked by the sweeping defeats.

"It is a catastrophic night for Republicans," Washington Examiner columnist Guy Benson reacted on Fox.

DEMOCRAT SEIZE HOUSE CONTROL IN STUNNING BLUE TSUNAMI, VOW RETRIBUTION AGAINST TRUMP ADMIN

Democrats have retaken both the House and the Senate in a major blowout in the 2026 midterms. (Fox News - Paul Steinhauser)

"Sometimes you get your a-- kicked, and deserve it. Tonight is one such time for the Republican Party," conservative radio host Buck Sexton reacted to the results on X. "Way too many mistakes. Bad messaging. Poor candidates. High prices. Unnecessary war that did not go as promised. We get up tomorrow and carry on. But there are lessons here."

"Tbh most Republican candidates this cycle were uninspiring, lazy, and thoroughly ineffective communicators. I’m not all that surprised by some of these outcomes," Trump advisor Alex Bruesewitz said.

HUGH HEWITT: THE GHOSTS OF 2006 ARE STIRRING — BUT WILL THEY CATCH THE GOP?

"[Trump] picked a bunch of the bad ones," commentator Mary Katharine Ham wrote on X of the losing candidates.

Many pointed to Trump, the war with Iran and the surge in gas prices as being responsible for the devastating losses for his party.

"Trump launched an unpopular and pointless war. Gas prices are too high. People can’t afford groceries. Trump abandoned the American First message. This is why Republicans are getting crushed. It’s very simple," The Daily Wire's Matt Walsh wrote.

"This will be the biggest national wipeout for Republicans since 2006, when voters brutally punished the GOP for an ill-advised and poorly planned war in the Middle East," The Federalist co-founder Sean Davis said.

However, conservative radio host Erick Erickson insisted the issues went far beyond the Iran war and gas prices.

"It was also the corruption. The incompetence. The tariffs. The playing nice with Russia. The impression of cruelty. The overly aggressive deportations. The accidental arrests of American citizens who were Hispanic. The arrogance. The ballroom. The reflecting poll. The golf courses. The arch. The Qatari 747. The aggressive redistricting push. The threats against enemies," Erickson listed.

The "Ruthless Podcast" hosts appeared on Fox News Channel and joked about leaning towards hard liquor as the night progressed.

"I don't think this was, at all, concerned with policy. This is a firm backlash," Josh Holmes told Fox News' Bret Baier.

"This is an absolute backlash from the voters," Comfortably Smug agreed. "They aren't concerned with the policies these Democrats have. They aren't concerned with any kind of vision for the future that the Democrats are offering or how they're going to fight inflation … They are angry, and they're making their voices heard."

"Ruthless" co-host Michael Duncan suggested there was a "dissonance" among voters separating the Democratic policies that were rejected under the Biden administration and that the GOP message "didn't resonate."

"Ultimately, at the end of the day, the present condition of the voters is what they vote on, not the scary thing you project into the future. And unfortunately, that's the problem for the Republican Party," Duncan said. "It didn't matter if it was a DSA candidate or [Annie] Andrews in South Carolina. They all moved up in a wave together, irrespective of that."

Trump did several interviews as the results rolled in, congratulating Democrats and saying he was willing to work with the party controlling Congress and also ready to use the veto.

Trump said he believed he had support for the war with Iran but felt voters weren't willing to put up with the "short-term" pain of higher gas prices. He also said he didn't feel like it was a personal defeat since he wasn't on the ballot.

"I think the Democrats did a good job," he told Fox News. "I really do. I think they did a good job. They fought hard. They've been fighting for a long time."

Fox News' Brian Flood contributed to this report.

title: Vance: Republicans Lost Midterms Because of Iran War
text:
WASHINGTON — Vice President JD Vance said Wednesday that Republicans lost the midterm election in decisive fashion because of the Iran war.

Vance published a lengthy tweet in the morning, saying that many who voted for Trump and himself in 2024 turned out, but voted for Democrats:

One of the things the data analysts on our side obsessed over was “composition”—whether the electorate looked close enough to 2024 for Republicans to win. And despite polls that showed a Democrat blowout, the data kept on telling us the same story: in some states turnout was merely OK, in other states it was downright amazing, and in no state was it catastrophic. There was a genuine sense of optimism on our team: our people were showing up.

So, I asked the smartest data guy I know, does that mean we’re going to shock the world? “No,” he told me. “We might do better than the polls suggest. But the data is telling us that a lot of Trump/Vance 2024 voters are pissed and planning to vote for the other guys. Our voters are turning out, but they may not vote for us.”

Well, that looks prophetic now. Our voters did show up. In Florida, for example, the electorate was 9 points more Republican than Democrat, just a couple points worse than 2024. Undoubtedly there were places we could have done better on turnout. But the main problem is not turnout. The main problem is that many people who voted for Trump/Vance in 2024 voted for Democrats in 2026.

Vance added that another pollster he trusts told him the GOP would get crushed on Tuesday because “lots of Trump 2024 voters were angry.” The pollster told Vance that four key moves would help these voters come back to the GOP: “1) End the war 2) Focus on cost of living/inflation 3) Put America First 4) Change our relationship to Israel.”

“Our voters showed up. And the above four reasons are why many of them voted for Democrats. This is according to a pollster who nailed the results,” Vance said.

He then emphasized that the reason Republicans lost is Iran:

In the next few months, there’s going to be a lot of gaslighting. Expect to hear any number of establishment politicians say the solution to our woes is amnesty. I’m open to the idea that we should change enforcement—by focusing more on businesses that hire illegal labor, for instance. But anyone pushing amnesty is lying to you.

The reason we lost is the war. The president himself said so last night.

If you’d like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so. Argue it was a worthwhile cost to pay. Agree or disagree, that’s at least honest.

But everyone knows why we lost. And any honest conversation about where we go from here must start there.

title: Trump’s Midterm Disaster | National Review
text:
President Donald Trump has sunk the GOP again. He did it in 2018, when the party lost the House, and in 2022, when a promised red wave fizzled. He did it again in the Georgia runoffs of January 2021, which cost the party the Senate. On Tuesday, Democrats took both chambers of Congress, riding a huge anti-Trump blue-nami.

The president’s rock-bottom approval ratings were the anchor that sank many good GOP candidates this week. Reuters/Ipsos recorded his approval at a record low of 31 percent in mid-October, the lowest of any president on record in a midterm election year, and his long-winded, meandering speeches in deep-red states in the last month of the campaign only highlighted the GOP’s Trump problem.

Consider what Republicans could have campaigned on. They had a border that was demonstrably more secure, a tax law that locked in 2017 gains, and a business-friendly regulatory climate that helped create a vibrant economy. These are real achievements, and conservatives should be proud of them. But they only matter if voters hear about them, and the president’s priorities ensured that the national conversation leading up to the election was about other things.

Two years ago, Trump campaigned on bringing costs down. Instead, the voters who handed him a second term watched tariffs (which are another form of taxes) and an ill-planned war in Iran inflate the cost of everything from groceries to gas. Trump then brazenly said he did not care about rising prices. Voters took note.

Then there is the Trump style of governance, which has always been widely disliked but that his most devoted supporters insist does not matter. It matters. Most Americans are not ideologues; they are normal people who want the government to function and the news to be boring. Instead, they got shutdown brinkmanship, presidential bombast, executive actions announced by social media post, forever wars, and support of murderous dictators like Vladimir Putin over democratic allies like Ukraine. Trump’s tendency to turn policy disputes into bitter personal feuds did not help. Many conservatives recoil from Trump’s chaotic government and tendency to do whatever is best financially for the Trump family.

The White House also made a cynical bet that the electorate could be bought. In September, Trump promised $5,000 to every American adult if Republicans won both chambers. Set aside the fiscal absurdity of promising checks to cure an inflation problem that borrowed money helps cause. The pitch tells you what the White House thinks of voters: They are customers to be bribed, not citizens to be persuaded.

Speaking of bribes, voters of both parties took offense at the overwhelming stench of corruption coming from the White House. Ambassadors demanding $100,000 payments. The president’s son getting a Russian oligarch to pay for his wedding celebrations. A MAGA insider reaping a $50 million contract for getting her foreign client a Trump pardon. The list goes on and on; its stench became impossible to ignore.

Then there were the stupid strategic blunders. Look no further than my home state of Texas, where an honorable and popular senator, John Cornyn, was derailed in the primary by an indicted felon who was impeached in the Texas House by his own party. Ken Paxton’s only claim to fame was being a hardcore MAGA Trump acolyte. Trump loves those who kiss his ring, and his full-throated endorsement of Paxton turned an all-but-certain Texas Senate reelection into a blowout loss that doomed many other good Texas GOP candidates. Trump’s gut instinct led him to back one of the most corrupt politicians in Texas history over the strong objections of virtually every GOP senator and leading Texas Republican. Stupidity and arrogance proved to be a fatal combination.

In the end, virtually all strongly pro-MAGA candidates lost, even in red states like Ohio (goodbye, Vivek), South Carolina (sorry, Lindsey), and Georgia (should have listened to Kemp). Many of the most pro-MAGA House members (alleged domestic abuser Max Miller, January 6 leader Scott Perry, and ever-Trumper Lauren Boebert) all lost in red districts. Voters just put a gigantic exclamation point on the end of the Trump era.

So, what happens now? Trump and his sycophants will blame the candidates, the media, redistricting, anything but himself. Indeed, Trump posted on Truth Social on Election Night that he would have won in a “landslide” if he had been on the ballot. So typical. Back in the real world, Tuesday’s results leave Republicans facing a decision we cannot put off, and it will shape the 2028 race starting today.

One path is more of the same: tariffs, inflation, and expanding deficits as permanent features of economic policy, governance by grievance and social media posts, and a party that exists mainly to serve oligarchs and demagogues. MAGA does have a loyal, if shrinking, base and an ability to win primaries. But it has now lost the House and Senate with a president whose approval sits in the low thirties. That is not a foundation for winning a general election in two years, and the voters have clearly said so.

The other path is a return to what made the Republican Party a governing force for decades: low taxes and restraint on spending, free trade that lowers prices rather than raises them, a federal government that does fewer things better, and a national defense strong enough to deter adversaries without having to go to war. None of this is exotic. It is the platform that won the Cold War, built our postwar prosperity, and repeatedly gave Americans a reason to trust the Republican Party. It is also, not incidentally, what voters seem to want when they complain about the cost of groceries and the state of the world.

The 2028 primaries will reveal which path the Republican Party chooses. A candidate who can credibly run as a traditional conservative, one who defends free markets, free trade, a smaller but more effective government, and a strong foreign policy — without all the chaos — will find an electorate that is hungry for exactly that. Mike Pence, Brian Kemp, Michael McCaul, and Glenn Younkin: take note. Trump uber-loyalists like Vice President JD Vance now have a much tougher path.

The genuine cost of Tuesday’s election is that Trump has once again taken a favorable set of conservative ideas and attached them to a political brand that the large majority of voters firmly reject. Limited government, secure borders, strong national defense, and economic growth are not losing ideas in general. They are losing right now because of who is carrying them. MAGA loyalists can keep pretending otherwise and continue to lose. Voters, as usual, have the last word. The GOP must now decide if it wants to be a permanent MAGA minority party or a big-tent conservative governing coalition in the style of Ronald Reagan.

U.S. Attorney Jeanine Pirro and other career prosecutors are heading up the investigation, a source familiar with the matter told NR.

Dhillon decided to resign after it became clear that she would not be considered for promotion, a DOJ source told NR.

Heidi Overton promises to make the FDA ‘the agency of the possible rather than the impossible.’

The GOP faces deep structural problems that only a new policy vision can fix.

title: Takeaways from the 2026 midterm elections
text:
The midterm elections turned out to be a brutal loss for Republicans as they lost control of both chambers of Congress on Tuesday.

The results can be viewed as a rejection of President Donald Trump’s agenda, which was undermined by the Iran war and rising costs this year. The result was a massive blue wave that took the White House by surprise.

Join Washington Examiner for unlimited access to the news, analysis, and commentary that matter most.

Though Democrats are now poised to control the House and Senate, Trump has expressed his intent to use his veto power for any Democrat-led bill that may cross his desk during his last two years in office.

Here are the major takeaways from Election Day as the results finish coming in.

Democrats took control of the House, surpassing the 218-seat threshold required for a majority. Democrats have secured 228 seats so far, which puts them higher than Republicans’ slim 218-seat majority in the 119th Congress.

When the House convenes for the next session, House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-LA) will make way for House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-NY) to take the top House post.

Democrats flipped the Senate, with Josh Turek’s victory in Iowa pushing the party over 50 seats. Turek won the seat by more than 4 points against Rep. Ashley Hinson (R-IA).

As of Wednesday morning, Democrats secured 54 seats in the chamber. This election cycle was a blue tsunami, significantly outpacing Republicans’ performance in the 2022 midterm elections.

Democrats pulled off multiple major upsets, such as in South Carolina. Sen. Darline Graham (R-SC) lost her bid for a first full term to Democrat Annie Andrews, who won by more than 4 points.

The president’s endorsement of Graham was expected to put her ahead in the red state. Andrews, however, managed to pull ahead. She will become South Carolina’s first Democratic senator in more than 20 years.

Texas also saw Democrats sweeping the elections, with Gina Hinojosa ousting three-term Gov. Greg Abbott (R-TX) and James Talarico beating state Attorney General Ken Paxton in the state’s highly competitive Senate contest.

The gubernatorial election results were finalized shortly after Abbott conceded the race, and Paxton did the same after his race was called. Hinojosa and Talarico, who became the first Democrats to be elected to their respective posts in over three decades, represent a sizable blue shift in Texas.

In Ohio, Democrat Amy Acton won the governor’s race by nearly six points over Vivek Ramaswamy. Her victory broke Republicans’ hold over the governor’s mansion, which is currently held by term-limited Gov. Mike DeWine (R-OH).

Ramaswamy’s campaign was likely impacted by the controversy involving its attack ad featuring Acton’s mother, Donna Arthur, who turned out to be a questionable source. The ad was released in the last 15 days before the general election.

The midterm elections also brought about a night of historic firsts, with major milestones regarding representation being achieved in U.S. politics.

In Georgia, Democratic candidate Keisha Lance Bottoms is set to become the state’s first black governor and the first black woman elected governor in the United States. She previously served as mayor of Atlanta and as a senior adviser in the Biden administration.

Bottoms, who defeated Republican contender Rick Jackson, also flipped the governor’s mansion in Georgia to Democrats for the first time since 1998.

Similarly, Rep. Byron Donalds (R-FL) will become Florida’s first black governor after narrowly outperforming Democratic opponent David Jolly.

Donalds’s victory in the gubernatorial race helped extend Republicans’ standing in Florida, which used to be a swing state.

Meanwhile, Hinojosa will become Texas’s first Latina governor and its first female governor since 1995. Abbott conceded the race.

In New Mexico, Democratic nominee Deb Haaland, who is of Native American descent, is on track to become the first indigenous woman elected governor of any U.S. state.

Rep. Chris Pappas (D-NH) is going to be the first openly gay man elected to the Senate. Sen. Tammy Baldwin (D-WI) was the first openly gay person elected to the Senate in 2012.

title: Midterms force a reckoning on Iran war
text:
▪ Outstanding Alaska, Mississippi ballots

The Democratic sweep that stunned much of Washington on Tuesday night could drastically shorten President Trump’s runway to end the war in Iran, which even he conceded was a driving force in the election blowout.

When Democrats take control of the House and Senate in January, they will have new leverage over Pentagon spending, and Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer (N.Y.) made clear that his party intends to use it.

“We are going to end the war,” Schumer said at a press conference.

“We have some Republicans already who have joined us in ending the war, and the Founding Fathers had the power of the purse as one of the ways of deterring a president who does war without the consent of the American people,” he continued.

The Trump administration has asked Congress for a $1.5 trillion defense budget for next year, including additional Pentagon spending through reconciliation. It has separately requested emergency funding to cover costs tied to the Iran war.

Some Republican lawmakers have reportedly begun talking about a year-end reconciliation bill that could include funding for the Iran war and several other GOP priorities.

That process could allow Republicans to approve the money without Democratic votes, but they have only a few weeks in session to agree on a package and get it through both chambers. They also have to address the Dec. 11 government funding deadline.

It’s unclear how many Republican lawmakers are willing to vote for more war funding after Tuesday’s losses. Both Trump and Vice President Vance said the war hurt their party at the polls.

“The reason we lost is the war. The president himself said so last night,” Vance wrote on social media. “If you’d like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so. Argue it was a worthwhile cost to pay.”

“But everyone knows why we lost,” he added. “And any honest conversation about where we go from here must start there.”

Trump did just that. He said he agreed with the vice president’s assessment but said he doesn’t regret getting involved in the war.

“I think it’s largely true because it drove the gasoline up a little bit, short term, and probably — that’s probably, it’s true,” Trump told reporters about Vance’s comments, during an event celebrating his White House ballroom. “But at the same time, if I had it to do again, I’d have to do it again because long term, it’s the only answer. You can’t let Iran have a nuclear weapon.”

Democrats could also demand accountability from the administration by bringing another war powers resolution. In June, both chambers adopted a concurrent resolution directing Trump to halt unauthorized military activity against Iran, but concurrent resolutions don’t get sent to the president’s desk, and the White House dismissed it as not having force of law.

Democrats this time could pass a joint resolution and send it to Trump for a signature. But if he vetoed the measure, it would take two-thirds of both chambers to override his decision. Even with their new majorities and growing unease over the war among some Republicans, Democrats would need substantial GOP support to override a veto.

Democrats have also indicated they intend to scrutinize the Pentagon and its chief, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand (D-N.Y.), who sits on the Senate Armed Services Committee, told Axios that Hegseth “will be forced to answer” for his “chaotic and incompetent leadership.”

He could face punitive measures even before Democrats take control, as Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.) is promising an impeachment vote when Congress returns this month, unless the Pentagon chief resigns first.

The shifting winds in Washington come as Trump weighs his next step on Iran, with The Hill reporting earlier this week that the president could be leaning toward resuming military activity in Iran over efforts to renew peace talks.

Iranian officials have cast the midterm results as a rejection of the war, but they are still bracing for Trump’s next move, warning the U.S. against more strikes but saying they are prepared to respond if necessary.

“Conscience or the cost of living, Americans said NO TO WAR, and ‌we endorse this message,” Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Qalibaf, Iran’s chief negotiator, wrote in a post on X.

Alexander Bolton has a new piece out for The Hill Insider on how Schumer and House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries (N.Y.) are already planning to use their majorities to constrain Trump’s agenda. High on that list, he reports, is the Iran war, which voters blame for high gas, diesel and grocery prices.

▪ CNN: What Trump’s setback could mean for Iran, Israel, Ukraine.

House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) looks on as President Trump speaks with reporters, Nov. 1, 2026, at Dubuque Regional Airport in Dubuque, Iowa, en route to a campaign rally. (Jacquelyn Martin, Associated Press)

NEXT MAN UP: House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) told his staff on a call Wednesday that he will not run for minority leader after the GOP lost the House, clearing the way for a potentially bitter fight over the party’s future.

House Majority Leader Steve Scalise (R-La.) and Rep. Jim Jordan (R-Ohio) are both expected to launch bids for the role, The Hill’s Sudiksha Kochi reports. The contest seems likely to pit the establishment (Scalise) against a more conservative wing of the conference (Jordan).

Trump didn’t pick sides when asked about the race to replace Johnson on Wednesday.

Meanwhile, Republican Study Committee Chair August Pfluger (R-Texas) is running against House Majority Whip Tom Emmer (R-Minn.) for the position of minority whip. Pfluger argued in a letter to his colleagues Wednesday that “new fresh ideas” and a leadership team with a plan to win back the majority in 2028 is needed.

Kochi notes that Johnson and Emmer’s tenures in their leadership positions have been marked by deep divisions within the GOP conference, including some times when conservative hard-liners blocked legislation from advancing to the floor.

▪ The Hill: Republicans sort through election carnage for a message in new era.

▪ The Hill: GOP House incumbents swept away in blue wave.

WAITING GAME: Democrats are assured of a comfortable Senate majority in the next session of Congress, but two key states remain uncalled.

Democrat Mary Peltola narrowly leads Sen. Dan Sullivan (R) in Alaska’s Senate race but is short of the majority she would need to avoid going to ranked-choice tabulation. Presuming that remains the case, that would mean that a couple more weeks could be needed before a winner is declared.

The true surprise nailbiter is Mississippi, where Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith (R) trails Democrat Scott Colom by just under 2,000 votes. Ballots are still coming in, and the state allows mail-in ballots to be counted as long as they’re postmarked by Election Day and received within five business days later.

The exact number of outstanding ballots is unknown. A close final result could land the contest in court, but as The Hill’s Sophie Brams and Zach Schonfeld note, Mississippi doesn’t have any law that provides for a recount in federal elections.

That essentially leaves it up to judges to determine how to resolve disputes.

▪ The Hill: Democrats broke GOP’s grip on Texas.

▪ The Hill: Democrats’ success boosts ranks of Hispanic caucus.

MARKET RALLY: The Dow Jones Industrial Average surged 1,569 points, or 3 percent, yesterday in its best post-midterm elections day since 1982, CNN reported, citing data from CFRA Research. Wednesday also marked the Dow’s largest gain since April 2025.

The S&P 500 rose 1.58 percent, in its second-biggest post-midterm gain since 1982. And the Nasdaq Composite rose 1.44 percent, in its biggest post-midterm gain since 2018.

A certain amount of stability that’s expected to come may be the cause.

“Wall Street loves divided government, because typically divided government doesn’t do anything, and it’s very much the case in this particular situation that it’s going to be very hard to do anything affirmative during the last two years of Trump’s administration,” Daniel Alpert, the executive chair at Westwood Capital, told The Hill’s Max Rego.

Oil prices also dropped sharply yesterday as bond yields fell, and investors weighed what the election results might mean for the future of the Iran war. Brent crude fell 8.7 percent to $94.62 a barrel, its lowest close in more than two months. Defense firms’ stocks also fell, with Lockheed Martin down nearly 7 percent.

▪ The Hill: Stocks rally after Democrats march to victory.

▪ The Hill: Stock futures soar after Democratic rout.

SPOT ON: Online prediction market platforms were able to predict with remarkable accuracy the outcomes of many midterm races Tuesday, often hours before the races were called by major TV networks, The Hill’s Julia Shapero and Dominick Mastrangelo report.

Despite the growing scrutiny prediction markets have faced on Capitol Hill, traders poured billions of dollars into platforms like Polymarket and Kalshi ahead of the election, gauging with striking accuracy the public’s perception of likely outcomes.

Kalshi said its markets had correctly predicted 98 percent of House, Senate, governor, attorney general, lieutenant governor and secretary of State races. Polymarket similarly said its midterm markets were accurate in 98.4 percent of resolved races, compared with the day before the election.

In many ways, the popularity of prediction markets has the potential to change the way people wait for results to come in.

“It’s now routinely hours between when prediction markets call it versus the TV networks,” Polymarket CEO Shayne Coplan wrote in a post on social platform X. “The networks hold out until absolute certainty, and the suspense keeps it entertaining all night. No knock to them, but now there’s Polymarket, and many people are realizing they want to know what’s happening in real time.”

Ross Dahlke, an expert in computational social sciences and a professor at the University of Wisconsin-Madison, noted prediction markets “seem to be highly accurate.”

“The markets just react so quickly to new information in a way that a lot of traditional media isn’t set up to do, particularly with their concern over accuracy, fact-checking — for better or for worse,” he told The Hill.

Pre-election polls similarly had a good night on Tuesday, having mostly projected Democratic gains, but they failed to capture the scale of the party’s sweeping victory. Morning Report’s Jared Gans talked to pollsters for a piece in The Hill Insider on why polls underestimated Democrats.

Rep. Richard Hudson (R-N.C.) speaks at the Republican convention on Sept. 10, 2026, in Dallas. (Alex Brandon, Associated Press)

DUMMYMANDER DOMINOES: North Carolina Republicans’ decision to redraw the state’s congressional lines has officially backfired as Democrats flipped multiple Republican-held seats that weren’t even on most observers’ radars.

Decision Desk HQ projected Wednesday that GOP Reps. Richard Hudson, Brad Knott, Addison McDowall and Tim Moore will lose their seats to Democratic challengers. That’s in addition to an open seat being vacated by GOP Rep. Chuck Edwards that Democrats also flipped.

Hudson’s loss is particularly notable as he serves as the chair of the National Republican Congressional Committee, the House GOP’s campaign arm.

Rep. Virginia Foxx is trying to hang on for another term, currently trailing Democrat Chuck Hubbard by less than 100 votes as counting continues.

Republicans in the state legislature pushed through a redistricting plan earlier this year to boost their odds at ousting Rep. Don Davis (D-N.C.), whom they have targeted for the past few cycles. Not only did Davis manage to hold on, but the GOP’s plan also ended up backfiring by watering down the party’s majority in redder districts.

Thanks in part to what’s being called the “dummymander,” Democrats will hold a majority of the state’s House seats for the first time in more than a decade.

This effect was arguably most pronounced in North Carolina but happened to some extent in other states as well. The Hill’s Mike Lillis breaks down for Insider where else the GOP’s redistricting plan backfired.

And finally … It’s Thursday, which means it’s time for the weekly news quiz!

Democrats put up a historic performance in this year’s midterms, having won at least 54 Senate seats and eyeing 250 seats or more in the House. This week’s quiz will look back at some of the memorable midterm waves for both parties.

How many seats in the House did Democrats net gain in the 1974 midterms in the aftermath of the Watergate scandal and Richard Nixon’s resignation?

What was the name of Newt Gingrich’s policy platform that he rode to the House Speakership during the so-called Republican Revolution of 1994?

What did George W. Bush refer to the 2006 midterms as for Republicans?

After the GOP’s sweeping victories in the 2010 midterms, Republicans easily won control of the House, while Democrats were able to hold the Senate. How long had it been since an election that yielded that split?

title: What Republicans' huge loss means for Trump
text:
Democrats just put President Donald Trump in a bind.

The party is projected to win commanding majorities in the House and Senate after thrashing Republicans in key races up and down the ballot across the country. The blue tsunami will knock Washington on its head and crush the Republican congressional bulwark that both supported and shielded Trump through the first two years of his term.

Follow CNBC's live coverage of the 2026 midterm election results

The midterm result snuffs out any chance Trump had of passing partisan legislation in the second half of his presidency. And many of the interests he has been able to pursue without Congress' input — including tariffs, the Iran war and an array of Washington-area construction projects — are sure to face sudden pushback from newly empowered Democratic majorities.

The paradigm shift hardly leaves Trump helpless, however. As president at a time of executive power expansion, Trump wields singular authorities that could stymie Democrats' efforts to pursue their own agendas.

But with his grip on the Capitol shriveling and his approval ratings scraping record lows in numerous polls, it's unclear how much support he'll be able to muster to fight the coming political battles.

Even before Election Day, analysts and pundits had contemplated a Democratic rout so decisive that it would force a reckoning for the GOP, and potentially even pose an existential threat to Trump's "Make America Great Again" movement.

Marc Short, chairman of Advancing American Freedom and onetime chief of staff to former Vice President Mike Pence, told CNBC on Tuesday afternoon that the GOP has moved away from its conservative foundations.

"We need a refresh right now," Short said in an interview. "We've lost our way."

Trump has been vague about what he hopes to achieve with the rest of his term. But he has shared a vision of how he might coexist with a Democratic majority, and it involves heavy use of the veto pen.

"It's one of the stronger powers that a president has," Trump said in a Fox News interview overnight. "They'll send over things that are insane, and I'll veto them."

"And after a couple of months of vetoes, they'll call and they'll say, 'How do we get this stuff done?' And we'll work together," he said, adding, "I have a lot of friends that are Democrats."

Trump has previously stated his willingness to veto reams of legislation that Democrats send across his desk. In a New York Post podcast interview released Monday, Trump said that if Republicans don't win, "I veto everything."

Pressed to detail his plans for the next two years, Trump touted his record and said, "The most important thing is to keep it going. It's going to get better and better and better, unless people come in that hate our country."

If that happens, "I guess I'll become Mr. Veto," Trump said.

He may soon get his chance: House Democrats, poised to be led by current Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries of New York, are planning to pass a flurry of bills as soon as they take the reins next January, CNBC has learned.

The legislative push, first reported by The New York Times, aims to show a united Democratic caucus taking quick action on the issues they were elected to solve, especially oppressively high costs on everything from gas to groceries.

In their first 100 hours after being sworn in, House Democrats plan to introduce bills reinstating the enhanced health insurance subsidies that expired under the GOP-held Congress, and reversing the Medicaid cuts Trump signed into law earlier this year.

Democrats also plan to push forward a bill that would undo Trump's sweeping tariffs and reassert Congress' role in setting import taxes. And they will again vote on legislation to end the war with Iran, or seek congressional authorization to keep it going.

But without Trump's approval, those bills may end up as little more than symbolic gestures, as Democrats will lack the two-thirds majorities in both chambers that are required to override a presidential veto without GOP help.

And there's no guarantee the bills will even make it out of Congress: Despite their landslide victories, Senate Democrats will still end up shy of the 60 votes required to bypass the chamber's filibuster rules for most legislation, giving Republicans key leverage in the minority.

Democrats also could feasibly benefit from Trump's vetoes in the long term. Forcing the president to shoot down numerous popular bills could give them fodder in the 2028 election.

It's far from clear whether Trump believes he can find compromise with Democrats on any of their initial legislative priorities.

But any potential for a working relationship with the opposition could be poisoned early on, as Democrats in both chambers are aggressively signaling their plans to launch politically charged investigations against Trump, his political and corporate allies and even his family members.

Winning control of House committees gives Democrats the ability to issue subpoenas under the current rules.

Rep. Robert Garcia, D-Calif., who is likely to chair the House Oversight Committee in the next Congress, said his panel will target the Trump family's business dealings, corporate corruption and alleged abuses by federal immigration agencies. He also plans to return focus to the Trump administration's handling of files related to notorious sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.

As results rolled in Tuesday night, Garcia summed up his plans in a two-word statement: "Lawyer up."

It's not just Garcia. Other Democrats have already demanded records from the Trump administration on a range of issues. Rep. Jamie Raskin, D-Md., for instance, last week accused Trump of using tariff exemptions to cut "sweetheart deals" for industries whose leaders have plied the president with gifts.

Senate Democrats have sent similar signals.

"They are going to need to plant new forests for all of the subpoenas we'll be printing," Sen. Ed Markey, D-Mass., said in an X post late Tuesday in response to a post, appearing to refer to tech executives.

The investigations are widely expected to consume much of the rest of Trump's term.

Trump has ample experience being targeted by Democrats, who impeached him twice in the House during his first presidential term.

But with his base of support appearing to erode inside and outside of Washington, Trump may have to face his political foes with a smaller arsenal than he's used to.

"I'm not expecting Republicans to revolt" against Trump following the midterm losses, AAF's Short told CNBC. "But I'm expecting some of them to quietly distance themselves."

title: Why did Republicans lose the midterm elections? GOP soul-searching begins after blowout.
text:
Washington — Widespread Republican losses in the midterm elections are roiling the GOP, prompting soul-searching over what went wrong and a brewing blame game that's expected to heat up as the party looks toward the next election.

From House and Senate races to governors' mansions, Republicans saw striking losses, both in battlegrounds and in places where the party saw significant support just two years ago. The victories dramatically shifted the balance of power in Washington, delivering Democrats a sizable majority in the House far beyond what was expected heading into Election Day, as well as a Senate majority larger than what the GOP has enjoyed for the last two years.

As Republicans process the results, including some GOP officials who have ambitions of their own in 2028, they're offering frank assessments of the shortcomings — and laying the groundwork for where the party heads next.

Throughout the country, as Republicans tried to rally support around their accomplishments over the last two years, the president's war in Iran loomed large. And in this week's elections, its impact on the economy and prices appeared to overshadow most everything else.

"The reason we lost is the war," Vice President JD Vance said in a candid post on social media that was among the first efforts from a top Republican to unpack the party's losses.

"If you'd like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so. Argue it was a worthwhile cost to pay," said Vance, who is widely seen as a possible presidential contender in 2028. "But everyone knows why we lost. And any honest conversation about where we go from here must start there."

Asked about the comments, President Trump told reporters that it's "largely true" that Republicans lost the House and Senate because war led to higher energy prices, agreeing with Vance. But he also argued that the war has been worthwhile.

"If I had to do it again, I'd have to do it again," Mr. Trump said.

Early in the war, Mr. Trump acknowledged that the vice president was "philosophically, a little bit different than me," and was "less enthusiastic about going" into Iran. Still, Vance has largely stood by Mr. Trump on Iran.

GOP Sen. Ted Cruz of Texas, who called the midterms a "Watergate-level repudiation," also cited the war, saying, "the Iran war has dragged on too long."

"It should have been brief, decisive, and over — it needs to end," said Cruz, who has vocally supported the war.

But Cruz pointed more broadly to the war's impact on prices, citing gas and diesel, along with the impacts of the president's trade policy, saying, "Tariffs have made everything too expensive."

Former Vice President Mike Pence also criticized Republicans' handling of the Iran war, but from the opposite direction, writing that the "unfinished war against Iran became an albatross around the necks of Republicans because Washington stopped short and pursued appeasement rather than allowing our troops to finish off the threat posed by the Iranian regime, once and for all."

More so than the war in Iran, voters nationally said cost of living was a major factor in their vote, according to CBS News exit polls.

Cruz said many GOP candidates this cycle seemed "like they didn't understand or they didn't care" about the cost of living. He said there's a "very real economic disconnect: Our K-shaped economy is a yawning divide," referring to the idea that some Americans' fortunes are on the upswing while others are pointing downward.

The Texas Republican cited Elon Musk becoming the world's first trillionaire, while at the same time, millions of Americans struggled to feed their families. And as data centers were constructed and the wealthiest people became even wealthier, he said Americans saw their electricity bills go up significantly in recent years.

"Understandably, people were pissed off," he said. "And elected Republicans didn't do enough to address their very real pain."

Democrats hammered Republicans over the cost of living, as economic populism became a key tenet of the cycle, while some candidates, like James Talarico in Texas, billed the fight as top-versus-bottom, rather than left-versus-right. Texas Republicans suffered one of the most striking routs of the midterms: Starting next year, Cruz will be one of the only Republican statewide elected officials in a state that was once viewed as almost imperviously red.

GOP Sen. John Cornyn of Texas, whose seat Talarico will take in the new year after Cornyn lost his primary to Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, lamented that after voters trusted Mr. Trump and the GOP to "protect their pocketbooks" in the 2024 elections, the president "misread his mandate."

"Voters wanted to retool our trading relationships, but got arbitrary 'Liberation Day' tariffs that raised prices without creating incentives for long-term reshoring," Cornyn wrote in a Wall Street Journal op-ed. "Voters wanted secure borders and peaceful streets, but got hyperaggressive immigration enforcement. The Iran conflict came with no attempt to persuade the public. And Mr. Trump signaled disconnection by focusing on sideshows like swimming-pool liners in the Reflecting Pool."

Cornyn added, "Americans elected the Donald Trump who put on the apron of the Golden Arches and got a plan for a Triumphal Arch instead."

Cornyn, who was formerly the No. 2 Senate Republican, also pointed to how corruption surged to a top issue for voters, "thanks to flawed midterm candidates and a parade of unsavory headlines out of Washington."

Democrats like Talarico worked hard to tie corruption to cost-of-living concerns expressed widely. And roughly nine in 10 voters nationally said government corruption was a major factor in their vote.

"Voters won't trust Republicans to cut fraud and scams out of government programs until we cut them out of our own ranks," Cornyn wrote. "Party leaders have to stop excusing the inexcusable and police our side of the aisle — or voters will continue to police it for us."

Beyond the cost-of-living concerns, some Republicans also pointed to an over-emphasis on culture war issues.

Outgoing Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis, who called the midterm outcomes as "close to an extension-level event for Republicans as we have seen probably in the last hundred years," said he knew Republicans were in trouble when he saw they were spending hundreds of millions of dollars on ads centering transgender issues.

"That was not the issue motivating voters, and it was kind of like an attempt to just scare Republicans to vote," DeSantis said at a news conference.

By late October, more than $180 million had been spent on ads that centered transgender-related attacks against Democrats, according to the Associated Press, reminiscent of the "Kamala is for they/them, Trump is for you" ads that blanketed the airwaves in the 2024 presidential election.

DeSantis — who has staked out conservative positions on transgender issues — argued the issue is no longer as potent, saying: "Four years ago, we were in the peak-woke era." But now, he argued, "the issues are different."

"Republicans, it seemed like — in some of the ads I was seeing, with how much money they were spending — they really were fighting yesterday's battles," he said.

As Republicans turned their attention to transgender and other culture-war issues, Democrats didn't give the attacks traction, shifting the focus at nearly every turn to affordability concerns. Some moderate Democrats in battleground states also voiced opposition to transgender athletes' participation in girls' sports, which may have neutralized some attacks.

But DeSantis also argued the election wasn't the result of voters having positive views of Democrats — exit polling shows voters had unfavorable opinions of both parties, though Republicans' favorability (40%) was lower than Democrats' (47%).

Instead, DeSantis said, it was a "rejection of Republicans in Washington." And that rebuke wasn't only aimed at the president, he argued, but also the GOP-controlled Congress, as voters became "frustrated with the lack of productivity from Republicans in the House and Senate."

"So it's really both sides of Pennsylvania Avenue," DeSantis said. "It's not just one."

title: 6 takeaways from Democrats' big wave on election night
text:
All the signs were pointing in Democrats' direction heading into election night.

But nothing indicated quite this level of a romp.

Democrats won the House and the Senate, and while that outcome was always a possibility, the depth and breadth of the Democratic victories were jaw-dropping.

Tuesday night was a reminder that the pendulum of American politics continues to swing, and politics is never permanent.

Here are six takeaways about what happened, why it happened and what it all means going forward:

President Trump's unpopularity has been a glaring warning sign for the Republican Party heading into election night. Since the Iran war, Trump's approval ratings slid from 48% to as low as 36% in an average of the polls.

A whopping 62% of voters in this election disapproved of his job as president, according to the voter poll commissioned by the broadcast networks and the Associated Press, which mixes pre-Election Day polling of early voters and Election Day exit polls.

Three-quarters of voters said they are either angry or dissatisfied with the direction of the country. A plurality said the economy was the most important issue, and two-thirds said Trump's policies have made economic conditions worse.

In addition to the economy, corruption rose as an issue in the last several months. The voter poll showed that 62% said Trump prioritizes his own interests more than the country's.

For all of the things that will be written about this election, the bottom line is that Trump waged the kind of war he said he wouldn't get into — one that is dragging on, raising gas prices and piling on people who were already feeling the pinch — and now he is paying the price.

If Trump was supposed to be the kingmaker in the 2028 Republican presidential primary, think again. These midterms will have heavy reverberations for the presidential election. It will likely mean more GOP candidates will enter the race, and they will be more likely to present a wider view of what the direction of the party could be — rather than simply trying to carry the Trump torch.

The fundamentals of this election seemed to mirror the 2006 midterms amid the Iraq war — the last time the Democrats won back both the House and Senate. Democratic gains in this election, though, were seen as possibly being limited by structural disadvantages — primarily through Republican efforts to tilt the playing by redistricting.

Trump strongly encouraged conservative-led states to redistrict over the last year, hoping to gain more Republican seats in the House — but that backfired, particularly in South Texas. There was always the possibility that incidentally weakening safe districts could make them competitive. Now that that's happened, it's a true cautionary tale of the "dummymander."

The reason Texas Republicans' efforts to gerrymander didn't pay off is because Latinos did not vote in this election the way they did in the 2024 presidential election.

In 2024, Trump only lost the group by 5 points. It moved toward Trump at the time, in large measure because they were upset with inflation and believed Trump would bring down prices.

Not only did that not happen over the last two years, Trump also angered many in the community because of aggressive deportation tactics that targeted more than just hardened criminals, as Trump promised.

In a real indictment of the Trump deportation policies, roughly 60% of respondents in the voter poll said they disapproved of Immigration and Customs Enforcement, or ICE. Sixty-eight percent of Hispanics disapproved of how ICE is handling its job.

To be clear, Latinos are not a monolith. Latinos in South Florida have different backgrounds and priorities than those in South Texas or those in California or New York. But the fact that the largest-growing group in the country swung strongly away from the president and Republicans makes them very important electorally — a true swing group in the country that is underrepresented at the polls and has a lot of power.

Democrats won in a lot of red states. That is important for the party heading into the 2028 presidential election. To have a real chance at expanding the presidential map, they need to figure out how to appeal to red-state and rural voters. They showed in this election they can do that, but they won't have Trump as their rocket fuel in this next presidential election.

The Lone Star State, for example, has been a majority-minority state for a while, and that demography had previously given Democrats false hope. So is Texas the new Georgia, or will it revert to its conservative roots?

The breadth of Democratic victories in Texas in this midterm is undeniable. They won up and down the ballot — Democrat James Talarico won by roughly 12 points, or 1.1 million votes, the first time Texas is sending a Democrat to the Senate since 1988; incoming Gov. Gina Hinojosa won by 7 percentage points, or almost 700,000 votes; they flipped two congressional districts, both of which were won by Trump in 2024 by at least 14 points; they won lieutenant governor; attorney general; railroad commissioner and more.

As they say in Texas, they beat 'em like a rented mule. But are Democrats renting power in the state or is it something bigger? There is going to be a lot of money spent in 2028 to see if the blue gains in Texas are more permanent. And a lot is on the line, because Texas has 40 electoral votes, and putting it in play legitimately for Democrats would reshape the electoral map in a way that would only be rivaled by the earthquake of a shift that was California going for Democrats starting in 1992. (Yes, California used to be a reliably Republican state, going for the GOP in all but one election between 1952 and 1988.)

By the way, a bonus lesson from this election is that money isn't everything. Republicans spent more than $413 million on the Texas Senate race — and lost.

Democrats have the opportunity to show they can authentically represent their states and try to hold onto these inroads they made in lots of red states and districts.

They were handed the keys to Congress, and people are going to expect results. New York Democratic Sen. Chuck Schumer, the once majority leader who may want to be in the job again, victoriously promised overnight that "relief is on the way."

But how? Even if Democrats have serious policy ideas to help fix economic problems in the country, they can't wave a magic wand. They won't have a filibuster-proof majority in the Senate, and they are unlikely to have an eager negotiating partner in congressional Republicans or Trump. Just before midnight on election night, Trump put out an image on his social media platform of a big red hat with the word "VETO" on it.

So Democrats are in danger of overpromising and underdelivering, which has become all too common in politics, and leads to voters becoming jaded. Democrats have to be careful with their messaging and how they govern. There will undoubtedly be more investigations and oversight of the Trump administration. But how far will they go? Another Trump impeachment attempt, for example, could be politically fraught.

No doubt, the GOP was soundly rejected Tuesday night, but Democrats aren't much better liked. The voter poll showed Republicans underwater with a 41% favorable and 59% unfavorable rating. Democrats were 47%-53%. Democrats had lower approval ratings earlier in Trump's second term, mostly because of disaffected Democrats. They rallied together to win in these midterms, but fissures on the left are simmering below the surface and are about to become far more apparent in the 2028 presidential Democratic primaries.

For a decade, polls have underestimated Republican support. In these elections, that was not the case. In fact, in some places they underestimated Democratic support.

For example, the national generic congressional ballot — the question of who people would vote for if the election was held the day of the poll — favored Democrats by about 8 percentage points. The voter poll looks like it turned out to be at least +13.

It's important to understand that it's hard to poll when the country has been going through as significant a political realignment as it has been in the Trump era.

title: Dummymander: The GOP's Bid to Rig the Midterm Map Failed Spectacularly
text:
In the height of the summer, as Republicans began to notice that voters were displeased with Donald Trump’s first year-and-change of governance, the president demanded that Texas redraw its congressional map in order to create five new Republican-controlled seats. “We are entitled to five more seats,” the president decided.

It turns out Republicans are entitled to nothing. The off-cycle gerrymandering effort that spread throughout other conservative states ended up actually costing the GOP seats.

Nine states managed to redraw their map in the gerrymandering war, including California,which redistricted in response to Trump’s Texas plan. Experts estimated that across the country more than a dozen members of the Congressional Black Caucus were targeted by Republicans in the push to eliminate Democratic seats. Not all states were successful, in states like Kansas and Indiana, efforts to gerrymander the map at the White House’s request fell short, either blocked by the state legislature or court challenges. Of the 15 seats ultimately redistricted by Republicans ahead of the election, Democrats kept 11 — including four of the targeted districts in Texas. In Florida, all four of the seats targeted by the Republican-controlled government were won by Democrats. Ohio Republicans not only failed to oust Reps. Marcy Kaptur and Greg Landsman, they lost several other GOP-controlled seats as well. Conservative-friendly redistricting efforts in Louisiana and Alabama also flopped. It was, as pundits have dubbed it, a spectacular case of “dummymandering.”

Republicans were aided by an AprilSupreme Court decisioninLouisiana v. Callaiswhich gutted civil rights protections against anti-minority gerrymandering, and instituted new requirements for states to prove discriminatory intent in order to challenge electoral maps. Across the South, Republican-controlled states targeted the districts of Black lawmakers, including in Louisiana, Alabama, North Carolina, and Florida. Rep. Cleo Fields (D-La.) — the congressman whose district was at the heart of the Callais case — told Rolling Stone in May that despite the efforts to the GOP to rig the midterms and future elections for themselves “we cannot let that discourage us about voting, because if we do that, what does that say to John Lewis? Who had his brains literally beaten on the Edmunds Pettus Bridge. What does it say to Rosa Parks and Fannie Lou Hamer and Martin Luther King? All these great civil rights leaders, both Black and white, what does it say to them if we give up now?”

And indeed, voters throughout the South and Southwest made their displeasure known. Latinos came out in force. In Georgia, Sen. Jon Ossoff (D-Ga.) easily won his bid for reelection. Former Atlanta Mayor Keisha Lance Bottoms was elected the state’s first Black and first female governor. While the race has not yet been called, Mississippi District Attorney Scott Colom is on track to become the first Black senator from the state since Reconstruction. Texas elected its first Latina governor.

All in all, Democrats will come out of the midterms with one of the largest congressional majorities in modern history, and the victories that took place on Tuesday will shape the politics of their respective states for years to come. To borrow a phrase from the president, the 2026 midterms were “too big to rig.”

title: The night Trump’s presidency changed
text:
A midterm the president made about himself delivered Democrats wins deep in red territory and left Republicans answering for the power they hold.

For the last decade, Donald Trump tormented Democrats and defied expectations of what it meant to lead and endure in American politics.

On Tuesday, the old rules finally caught up with him.

Trump wasn’t on the ballot, but he made the midterms emphatically about himself, urging his supporters to turn out as if he were. After a decade in which he dominated the national narrative, the voters who had sided with him so often before appear not to have followed him en masse.

Democrats were projected to retake both the House and the Senate from the Trump-led GOP. They won governor’s races in red states and were closing in on upsets in deeply conservative congressional districts that, just days earlier, had looked all but unwinnable.

Plenty of races remained uncalled at 1 a.m. But the early returns pointed to one of the best nights for Democrats — if not the best — since Trump ran for the White House in 2016.

If those projections hold, the rest of Trump’s term will look very different. A Democratic House and Senate would be able to stall his agenda and investigate his administration, and the Senate would decide the fate of his nominees, including to the federal courts. That could be a significant check on a president who has already reshaped the Supreme Court.

The night also suggested that Trump’s appeal doesn’t transfer. Candidates he embraced or campaigned for lost in deep-red Kansas and South Carolina. Vivek Ramaswamy, an ardent ally of the president, lost the Ohio governor’s race. Trump’s conservative magic, it turns out, doesn’t extend to the candidates further down the ballot. That’s an uncomfortable reality for a party that has remade itself around one man.

His choices also proved costly. In Texas, Trump embraced the state’s impeached and acquitted attorney general, Ken Paxton, over a Republican incumbent who had won many times before. The party spent a fortune trying to save Paxton’s campaign, making it the most expensive race in the country this cycle. He lost anyway.

And Democrats found they could make a case in far more of the map than recent elections suggested. The party won statewide in Texas, Iowa, Ohio, Kansas and South Carolina, places that had long looked out of reach, in some cases breaking Republican winning streaks that stretched back decades.

Democrats also made history. In Georgia, Keisha Lance Bottoms, the former Democratic mayor of Atlanta, was elected the first Black woman governor in the nation’s history. She defeated a wealthy Republican who had campaigned on becoming Trump’s “favorite governor.”

In Ohio, which Trump carried by double digits two years ago, the state’s pandemic-era health director won as a Democrat, defeating Ramaswamy. Meanwhile, Sherrod Brown, the Democratic senator who lost his seat in 2024, won his way back to Washington in a special election for the seat JD Vance gave up when Trump elevated him to the vice presidency.

In South Carolina, Democrats defeated Darline Graham, the sister of the late Sen. Lindsey Graham, whose unexpected death this summer led to her appointment to serve out what little remained of his term. Trump and his allies spent precious time, money and attention trying to win her more than a brief stay in the Senate. South Carolina hadn’t sent a Democrat to the Senate since 1998. Now pediatrician Annie Andrews has changed that.

And in ruby-red Kansas, where Trump campaigned shortly before Election Day, Republicans lost a U.S. Senate race for the first time since 1932, the year Franklin D. Roosevelt was first elected president.

Election Day 2026 marked a sharp break from most of the Trump era. He stunned Democrats and the Republican establishment alike when he defeated Hillary Clinton in 2016. That night left a glass ceiling intact and a Democratic Party that has been afraid of its own shadow ever since.

Democrats won the House in the 2018 midterms but lost ground in the Senate. They captured unified control of Washington in 2020, as Trump tried to overturn his clear loss and a mob of his supporters violently attempted to subvert the peaceful transfer of power.

But Democrats’ uneven handling of the economy and immigration gave Trump ample opportunity for a comeback. He seized it, his deep influence among Republicans almost untouched, and returned to the White House in indisputable fashion in 2024, leaving the Democratic Party fractured, reeling and pointing fingers.

Republicans had unified control of Washington, and Trump, having swept every presidential battleground state, was ascendant. But he and his party were soon bedeviled by the same economic messaging woes that had undone the last Democratic administration.

They turned immigration, which had been a winning issue for them, into a national reckoning over aggressive and violent enforcement tactics that left Americans dead. The president tumbled into the Iran War. And the cost-of-living woes he once could have pinned on his predecessor quickly became indistinguishable from the consequences of his own decisions.

Midterms are often brutal on the incumbent president’s party. But the wins — and surprisingly narrow losses — that voters delivered Democrats on Tuesday suggested something bigger than the usual midterm backlash.

Singular as he has become in American politics, Trump also benefited from the zeitgeist he stepped into a decade ago. The 2010 tea party wave had energized Republicans around political outsiders, and the rise of social media allowed misinformation and conspiracy theories to spread far and wide.

But everything new eventually grows old. Now even Trump and his Republican allies must contend with the recriminations that come with holding all that power, rather than promising they could do better if given the chance.

Hunter Woodall covers politics for MS NOW. He’s reported on politics and presidential campaigns for The Associated Press and CBS News and reported on Congress for The Minnesota Star Tribune.

title: 4 takeaways after Democrats’ big night in New York
text:
Tuesday night’s blue tsunami fortified Democrats' dominance in New York — and boosted their influence around the country.

Gov. Kathy Hochul cruised to re-election over Nassau County Executive Bruce Blakeman with the widest margin for a New York governor since 2018, according to unofficial results. Democrats expanded their already large majorities in both the state Senate and state Assembly. And Mayor Zohran Mamdani saw his “affordability” message successfully deployed by Democrats to score historic wins from Texas to Maine.

Here are four takeaways from election night:

The governor has spent the last four years dogged by criticism that she dragged down the Democratic ticket with her narrower-than-expected win in 2022, when she defeated Lee Zeldin by just six points. But Hochul silenced those critics Tuesday night, with unofficial results showing a 20-plus-point drubbing of Blakeman. That included winning Blakeman’s own Nassau County.

Hochul bet big on her key alliance with Mamdani, that delivering on their shared promise to expand free childcare would energize the party’s young, progressive base. At the same time she cast herself as a moderate and level-headed foil to President Donald Trump, pushing back on his hardline immigration enforcement and trade war with Canada.

Hochul now goes into her second full term with goodwill, a robust fundraising machine and a mandate. It remains to be seen whether her margin of victory changed her political calculus on top progressive priorities like taxing the rich.

Over at Hochul’s victory party in midtown Manhattan, the star speaker of the night wasn’t the governor, but Mamdani.

Mamdani praised Hochul for embracing progressive policy ideas like universal childcare, and for her willingness to partner with him. But he drew a direct connection between Democrats’ triumphs across the country on a message of affordability and his own election last year.

“We have begun the work of transforming our party and making it belong to working people once again,” he said.

There was an obvious sign New York Republicans knew they were in for a bad night at the Long Island banquet hall where Blakeman held his election party: no TVs broadcasting election results. Instead, Frank Sinatra’s “My Way” blasted over the speakers.

Afterward, Blakeman delivered a brief concession speech, and some attendees continued to chat and order drinks at the bar as if nothing happened. Others sank into denial. “There had to be some shenanigans,” said Rosalie Cancellarich of Floral Park. “Am I saying it was rigged? I don’t know.”

The party has a steep uphill climb back to power — Republicans haven’t won statewide office in New York since Gov. George Pataki was re-elected in 2002. The GOP playbook focused on crime and illegal immigration — which Rep. Mike Lawler and Blakeman both used — was a dud. The party is in for some soul-searching ahead of 2028.

Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez has said she would wait until after the Midterms to decide whether to run for president or Senate. Tuesday night’s blue tsunami undoubtedly strengthens a case that she has a path to the White House. The congresswoman previously said that Abdul El-Sayed’s election in Michigan would portend a huge win for progressive movement, and that it could "break open the entire political calculus in America.”

Adding to the intrigue, Ocasio-Cortez’s campaign released a memo on Tuesday touting her accomplishments and concluding that the congressmember has “proven herself to be one of the most effective voices in the country for America’s working class.“

Ocasio-Cortez stayed out of the spotlight on election night, but she’ll now be fielding a lot of questions about her future. She won her fifth term in office with a commanding margin over her Republican opponent Diamant Hysenaj.

Some of her constituents were already mulling whether it might be the last time she asks voters to return her to the House.

Walter Wuthmann is a reporter covering public safety and the legal system.

Republicans’ “anti-city” agenda was rejected by voters, MTA Chair Janno Lieber said.
