title: 5 election takeaways: Democrats win big across New York
text:
New York Comptroller Tom DiNapoli, left, New York Gov. Kathy Hochul, Lt. Gov. candidate Adrienne Adams and state Attorney General Letitia James celebrate during an election night event on Tuesday in New York.

U.S. House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries and U.S. Senate Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer, both Democrats from Brooklyn, will lead their chambers unless Democrats choose new leaders before next year.

Gov. Kathy Hochul closed out her campaign this week in New York City, where turnout in support of her reelection surged compared to 2022.

Senate Majority Leader Andrea Stewart-Cousins is expected to add at least five new members to the Democratic conference next year.

ALBANY — Democrats in New York tightened their grip on power in this year’s elections, reelecting their full slate of statewide candidates, securing a supermajority in the state Senate and flipping a GOP-held U.S. House seat as a blue wave swept Democrats into control of Congress.

Jay Jacobs, the longtime chair of the New York State Democratic Party, said the results were a repudiation of President Donald J. Trump and his policies.

“We owe a debt of gratitude to Donald Trump,” Jacobs said. “People said enough’s enough. They were outraged by a lot of the things that were going on and they came out in large numbers and sent Washington a message.”

There are twice as many enrolled Democrats as Republicans in New York. But Democrats still exceeded expectations in various races around the state.

Here are five takeaways from election night.

Gov. Kathy Hochul won her first full term in 2022 by less than seven points, the closest margin of victory in a gubernatorial election since 1994, when former Gov. George Pataki, a Republican, narrowly defeated then-incumbent Gov. Mario Cuomo, a Democrat.

Hochul roughly tripled that margin, besting Republican Nassau County Executive Bruce Blakeman by nearly 20 points, according to results Wednesday morning from the state Board of Elections. She even led in Blakeman’s home county.

“This is how we take back our country,” Hochul told a cheering crowd in Manhattan. “Think about the generations of women who could only dream of this opportunity — women who knocked on doors that wouldn’t open, who fought for seats at tables where thy weren’t welcome. This night we stand on their shoulders.”

The governor had said her goal was to earn enough votes to help Democrats retake control of the House of Representatives. Her showing helped Democrat Cait Conley unseat Republican U.S. Rep. Mike Lawler in the 17th District, which covers the lower Hudson Valley.

Siena Research Institute polls of likely voters showed Hochul with a nine-point lead over Blakeman in September and a 14-point lead in late October. Parkside Group co-founder Evan Stavisky, a Democratic political consultant, said Hochul benefited from a “blue tsunami.”

“Kathy Hochul outperformed her polling by nearly 10 points. That is a tremendous accomplishment,” he said. “She did great and a rising tide lifted all boats.”

Hochul secured about 3.4 million votes compared to the 3.1 million she had four years ago, according to the state Board of Elections. Blakeman got 2.3 million votes — less than the 2.7 million ballots that were cast in 2022 for Hochul’s previous GOP opponent, former U.S. Rep. Lee Zeldin, who’s now head of the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency.

The exact margin and vote tallies hadn’t been fully finalized by Wednesday morning. The figures don’t include thousands of votes from Westchester County, where tabulation of votes was delayed by malfunctioning ballot scanners.

Hochul did better in the state’s largest Democratic bastion, New York City, compared to the last two election cycles.

She secured 75% of the vote in the five boroughs, which translates to about a quarter million more votes than she received in the city four years ago. When she won four years ago, Hochul garnered about 69% of the vote in New York City while Zeldin won nearly 30%. At the same time, Blakeman’s share dropped compared to Zeldin. The county executive won about 74,000 fewer votes than Zeldin in the five boroughs.

Hochul secured key endorsements in New York City this year and spent her final days campaigning in Brooklyn and Queens. New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, a darling of progressives, campaigned with the governor and released social media videos urging people to support her.

“Gov. Hochul has led with a recognition that our highest obligation is not to our factions, but to our futures,” the democratic socialist mayor said at Hochul’s election night party. Mamdani added that his dealings with Hochul are markedly different than the drama that historically surrounds governor-mayor relationships.

Blakeman expected a boost from Long Island’s Nassau and Suffolk counties that never materialized.

Hochul finished ahead of Blakeman in his home county by about 4,000 votes — a small but symbolic victory in a populous region where just under half a million ballots were cast. The Democratic governor had a similar margin of victory in Suffolk County, which was Zeldin’s base in 2022.

Zeldin won Nassau and Suffolk counties by almost 149,000 votes in 2022. This year, Blakeman is on track to lose Long Island by around 8,000 votes. He conceded the race to a crowd of supporters in Nassau County.

“You win some, you lose some,” Blakeman said. “The fact of the matter is, now we pull together, we move forward, we have the best interest of the people in our heart.”

Michael Dawidziak, a Long Island-based political consultant, said candidates running for other offices were hoping Blakeman would have a stronger showing.

“He hammered home the MAGA talking points at the expense of other things that could have excited the suburbs on Long Island and elsewhere,” said Dawidziak, whose clients often include Republicans.

Jacobs, who is also the Nassau County Democratic chairman, said the results show that Zeldin’s showing didn’t signal a permanent shift.

“What happened in Nassau and Suffolk counties show the commentators after the last gubernatorial election were wrong,” Jacobs said. “Long Island hasn’t gone red, it’s still strictly purple.”

Early returns show Hochul also won back six other counties that she lost to Zeldin in 2022: Broome, Dutchess, Orange, Rensselaer, Rockland and Saratoga counties.

Democrats only needed to flip one seat from Republicans in the state Senate to regain a supermajority, which occurs when one party holds more than two-thirds of the chamber’s seats.

A supermajority will give Democrats the numbers they would need to override a veto from Hochul without relying on Republican support. Such a maneuver requires parallel action in the state Assembly, where Democrats already had a supermajority.

Legislators have never attempted to override one of Hochul’s vetoes. But the practical effect of such a large majority is the breathing room it affords Democrats to advance bills that some members of their party caucus might oppose.

All Senate Democratic incumbents were reelected, and the party flipped at least five seats from the chamber’s Republicans.

“I am deeply grateful for the trust New Yorkers continue to place in our Senate majority,” said state Senate Majority Leader Andrea Stewart-Cousins. “This achievement reflects the strength of our diverse coalition, representing communities from our largest cities to our smallest towns, and our shared commitment to moving New York forward.”

While Stewart-Cousins will lead the conference, it was state Sen. Shelley Mayer, a Yonkers Democrat, who led their election efforts this year.

On Long Island, Democrat Chris Murray pulled out a surprise win over incumbent Republican state Sen. Anthony Palumbo. In Brooklyn, Democrat Larry ousted incumbent Republican state Sen. Steve Chan, who had flipped the seat two years ago.

In the Hudson Valley, two incumbent Republicans in the state Senate lost their races. Democrat Lisa Kaul defeated state Sen. Rob Rolison, who had been a top target of the conference, and Nyack Mayor Joe Rand defeated state Sen. Bill Weber.

And in the Capital Region, Democrat Sarah Rogerson defeated state Sen. Jim Tedisco, a Republican and longtime state lawmaker who was first elected to the state Senate in 2016 after serving 34 years in the state Assembly.

That will give Democrats at least 46 seats in the chamber. Republicans will have 17 at most after losing the majority as recently as 2018.

There are two remaining races in the Capital District and on Long Island that are too close to call.

Republicans in the state Senate did not immediately release a statement on the results from Tuesday night.

Two Democrats from New York are also poised for power at the U.S. Capitol after their party flipped control of the U.S. House and Senate on Tuesday night.

While Schumer already served as majority leader when Democrats had razor-thin control of the U.S. Senate during the administration of former President Joseph R. Biden, Tuesday’s results will give him a firmer grip on power.

“The American people reduced the red brick wall to a pile of bricks,” Schumer said Tuesday night. “And as a result, there is now a generational remake of the Senate map that is going to change America now and on into the future.”

He spoke about how Republicans had “followed Trump over the cliff” toward their defeat Tuesday night.

Jeffries is poised to become the first Black person and first New Yorker to serve as speaker of the House. He said on Tuesday night that Democrats in the chamber would seek to reverse Republican-backed changes to Medicaid eligibility standards and pledged that his conference would focus on bringing down costs.

“This is a change election and we understand as House Democrats that we need to deliver dramatic change,” Jeffries said. “Things are broken.”

Jeffries also said Democrats would “bring accountability to those who have visited unprecedented corruption in this country,” saying federal officials have been “focused on enriching themselves” and their families.

“We understand that trust has been broken between the Congress and the American people and we’re going to work hard to restore it,” Jeffries said.

title: New York Gov. Hochul wins reelection to second term
text:
New York Gov. Kathy Hochul cruised to a win Tuesday in her bid for a second full term, swatting away a challenge from Republican opponent Bruce Blakeman by relentlessly linking him to President Donald Trump.

Hochul, a centrist Democrat from Buffalo, focused much of her campaign on her record on pocketbook issues, using her robust war chest to air $30 million worth of ads touting her push to send energy rebate checks to New Yorkers, pause data center construction and expand access to childcare.

But the governor — on the campaign trail, on the debate stage and in many of her ads — rarely missed a chance to highlight Blakeman’s longstanding friendship with Trump, a strategy meant to capitalize on the roughly two-thirds of New York voters who say they view the president unfavorably in public-opinion polls. Blakeman did not try much to distance himself from Trump, appearing with the president at multiple rallies and events.

The Associated Press declared Hochul winner right after polls closed.

“There’s a through line between a lot of the pain people are feeling and the frustration with the policies out of Washington and Donald Trump,” Hochul told reporters in Albany last week. “Bruce Blakeman said he would bring those policies right here to New York, and that's what voters are rejecting right now.”

Hochul, 68, became New York’s first female governor in 2021 following the resignation of then-Gov. Andrew Cuomo. She was elected to a full term in 2022, winning by a narrower-than-expected 6-point margin over Republican Lee Zeldin.

She spent decades working her way up through local government after winning her first election to the town board in the Buffalo suburb of Hamburg in 1994. Later, she became Erie County clerk and briefly served as a congressmember in a conservative-leaning western New York district before she was elected Cuomo’s lieutenant governor in 2014.

On the campaign trail, Hochul leaned into her place in history, often calling herself “New York’s first mom governor” or “first grandma governor.” She said that perspective helped inform major policies that headlined her five years in office — a ban on smartphones in schools, an expansion of free school meals and her push to expand childcare, among them.

Blakeman painted Hochul as soft on crime and immigration, faulting her for signing into law a measure restricting local governments — including Nassau County — from cooperating with federal immigration agents. He pledged to cut income taxes and utility bills, blaming Hochul for rising rates above the national average.

“ I believe she's got her priorities upside down,” Blakeman said during his lone debate with Hochul last month. “So I'm gonna ask you to vote for change. What have you got to lose?”

But Blakeman’s message couldn't break through in a state with twice as many Democrats as Republicans. He was hurt, in part, by a struggle to keep pace with Hochul’s fundraising, particularly in the critical final weeks of the campaign. He campaigned in lockstep with Trump, who is historically unpopular in New York due to the war in Iran, rising gas prices and the cost of living.

Blakeman’s focus on immigration enforcement came as polls showed voters are more likely to trust Democrats on immigration policy. Immigration had long been a winning issue for the GOP, but Trump’s second term has been marked by an aggressive crackdown that’s played out in viral videos from Chicago, Minneapolis and elsewhere. In the weeks before the election, an ICE agent shot a Dominican man through the neck in Upper Manhattan in broad daylight. The man was behind the wheel, with his 5-year-old son in the backseat.

With the loss, the GOP still hasn’t won a statewide election in New York since then-Gov. George Pataki won his third and final term in 2002.

Hochul has largely maintained her moderate stance as her party shifts left, steadfastly refusing to raise income taxes on the wealthy despite an ongoing push from the Democratic Socialists of America and other left-leaning organizations that have grown in prominence following the 2025 election of New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani.

Yet Hochul has maintained a strong working relationship with Mamdani, who campaigned with the governor and encouraged his following of young, Democratic voters to vote for her.

“ I think what I'm stepping out to do is to acknowledge the governor's leadership,” Mamdani said during a campaign stop with Hochul in McCarren Park in Brooklyn. “She has been a partner, not just for me, but a partner for the entire city.”

Hochul will return to Albany with a strong Democratic majority in both houses of the state Legislature, just as she had during her first five years as governor.

She has said she intends to continue her push for universal childcare and pro-housing policies at the Capitol in 2027, as well as expanding the state’s energy portfolio to include more nuclear power as the grid struggles to keep up with demand. She has also said she intends to run for a third full term in 2030.

“I have to build more energy sources to drive down the costs and keep us from being in a place where we're perilously close to having the lights turn out,” Hochul said last week. “But also, I'm going to build more housing. I'm going to have a massive plan again for the next five years that is going to finally get to a place where people can say, ‘I can afford a home.’”

Hochul’s race headline three statewide contests this year, with Attorney General Letitia James facing off against Republican Saritha Komatireddy and Comptroller Thomas DiNapoli facing Republican Joseph Hernandez.

Results in those races and in key congressional races across the state continued to trickle in late Tuesday night.

title: New York turns deeper blue as Democrats add five Senate seats and near supermajority
text:
New York was a wave of blue as Democrats were re-elected in statewide races.

“I think what we saw nationally is certainly personified right here in New York, a very blue state to begin with,” said Dr. Leonard Cutler, Professor of Political Science at Siena University.

New York Democrats added five more Senate seats; incumbent Republican Senator Jim Tedisco lost to newcomer Sarah Rogerson, a Democrat.

Several Assembly seats also flipped; incumbent Assemblyman Scott Bendett lost to Chloe Pierce. The state race results led to a Democratic supermajority.

“You know, the course of the session with a supermajority, you have the ability to override a governor's veto,” said Dr. Cutler. “That may very well be tested on major priorities of the Democratic Houses and leadership.”

Across the nation, seats in Congress were flipped, and more Democrats won governor races in decades. Those races begin right at home, says Cutler.

“So building at the grassroots with mayoralties, with state legislative races, with the governorships, and that's the future for your national officeholders,” said Cutler.

title: Cait Conley unseats Mike Lawler in tightly contested Hudson Valley House race
text:
Democrat Cait Conley defeated Rep. Mike Lawler in New York's 17th Congressional District despite an Election Day mired by issues at polling places in Westchester County.

Conley, an Army veteran and national security official, led Lawler, a two-term Republican congressman, by more than 11,800 votes as of 11:15 p.m., according to the Associated Press. That tally didn't include machines throughout Westchester County, where Conley was expected to win.

"When all of the votes are counted tomorrow in Westchester, it's gonna be pretty clear that we will be short," Lawler said during a concession speech Tuesday evening.

"I'm exceptionally proud of my record," Lawler said. "Despite the election results tonight, I am extremely grateful for the opportunity to have served in this capacity to have represented the community I was born and raised in, that I am raising my family in," he said.

The contest in Rockland, Putnam and Westchester counties had gained national attention because it was widely considered a swing district with control of Congress at stake.

But a problem involving paper ballots that prevented voting machines from accepting them caused havoc starting Tuesday morning, leading voting to continue only through emergency ballot procedures and the state and county election boards to work on deploying replacements.

The issue was caused by a late update to the “county's election programming” made due to a change affecting a contest in a municipality, which election machines did not recognize, the New York State Board of Elections said.

A board spokesperson said, "The issue was a mismatch between the printed ballots and the technology used by the machines to process them."

The board said every valid vote would be counted.

“Completed ballots are securely maintained under bipartisan oversight and will be scanned and counted in accordance with established procedures. Restoring scanning capability will also allow emergency ballots cast earlier in the day to be processed as part of the established counting process,” it said.

Lawler was running for a third two-year term in Congress. But he sometimes found himself on the defensive on the campaign trail this year amid a difficult political climate for Republicans.

While he campaigned as a moderate willing to break with President Donald Trump, who has received poor marks from voters on affordability and the war in Iran, Conley repeatedly tied him to not only the president but also Elon Musk. On the other hand, Lawler tried to link Conley to New York City’s Democratic Socialists of America.

The two also sparred over campaign financing and cost-of-living issues.

title: Dems increase majority in Dutchess Legislature
text:
POUGHKEEPSIE – The 2025 election included all 25 seats on the Dutchess County Legislature. The legislature usually serves two-year terms, but a change in State Election Law that moved elections to “even years” required all 25 seats to be up for election again this year. In the 2025 election, Democrats took control of the legislature, and many Republicans who lost campaigned this year to return to office.

Unofficial results indicate Democrats flipped one seat from Republicans, increasing their majority to 16, with only nine Republicans winning.

Of the 25 races, 17 were competitive, while seven lawmakers were unopposed and one seat was open because Lisa Kaul ran for State Senate against Sen. Rob Rolison. Democrat Tonya Speed ran for the District 6 seat Lisa Kaul vacated.

Democratic Legislators Brendan Lawler (District 4), Craig Brendli (District 8), Brenna Kearney (District 11), Chairwoman Yvette Valdes Smith (District 16), Molly Rhodes (District 18), Chris Drago (District 19), Kris Munn (District 20) all ran unopposed.

The unofficial results for the 17 Dutchess County Legislature races are as follows:

District 1 Democrat Trevor Redl defeated Republican Bob Gorman in a rematch from 2025. 2,049 to 972.

District 2 Democrat Emma Arnoff fended off a challenge from Republican Anne Burger. 2,748 to 2,383.

District 3 Democrat David Siegel flipped the district, defeating Minority Leader Mike Polasek. 2,508 to 2,444.

District 5 A rematch from 2025, with Democrat Anna Shah victorious over Tony D’Aquanni. 2,677 to 2,004.

District 7 Democrat Trish Prunty and Republican Lew Darrow met for a rematch, with Darrow winning again. 2,304 to 2,268

District 9 Majority Leader Barrington Atkins fended off a challenge from Republican Aaron Scott. 1,785 to 464.

District 10 An open seat after Democrat Randy Johnson chose not to seek re-election. Democrat Nakia Simmons handily defeated Republican Shanta Persad Saeteros. 1,443 to 196.

District 12 Democrat Anthony Giaccone lost to Minority Whip John Metzger. 2,919 to 2,065.

District 13 Democrat Keith Odums once again lost to the 2025 winner, Kevin Giles, a Republican. 2,752 to 2,251.

District 14 Another 2025 rematch with Democrat Alix Winsby fending off a challenge from her predecessor, Lynne Miele-Versaci. 2,113 to 1,741.

District 15 Incumbent Republican Rob Faust narrowly defeated Democrat Kyle Fendrich. 2,244 to 2,238.

District 17 Incumbent Republican Doug McHoul defeated Democrat Mike Schade. 2,477 to 2,379.

District 21 Republican incumbent Stephen Caswell fended off a challenge from Democrat Francine Caracappa. 2,778 to 2,109.

District 22 Democrat Heidi Tucci lost to incumbent Republican Joseph Tresca.

District 23 Democrat Marty Mygan lost to Republican incumbent Chris Rolison. 2,781 to 2,076.

District 24 Republican incumbent Andrew House defeated Democrat August Uribe. 2,199 to 1,788.

District 25 Democratic incumbent Eric Alexander put down a challenge from Republican Stefanie Hubert. 2,583 to 2,143.
